title: Streamable HTTP and the 2026-07-28 spec: stateless by design

concept.heading: Over HTTP, every request must carry everything the server needs
paragraphs: stdio is one host, one subprocess, one machine. Streamable HTTP is what you deploy: the server is a web app at /mcp and any client on the network posts JSON-RPC to it. The 2026-07-28 spec removed the initialize handshake from this transport: each request carries the protocol version, the client's capabilities and identity in _meta (and MCP-Protocol-Version plus mcp-method headers), the server answers server/discover with the versions it speaks, and there is no session id. HTTP+SSE, the older transport, is deprecated with removal after July 2027.

Stateless matters for a small nonprofit more than for anyone: a free host restarts your process without warning, a laptop lid drops a connection, two copies may run at once. If nothing has to be remembered between requests, all of that is fine. State that genuinely must persist (tasks, approvals, dedupe keys) goes in a database in Module 5, never in the server's memory.

The SDK does the protocol work: streamable_http_app(stateless_http=True, json_response=True) wraps your server as a Starlette app and uvicorn serves it. The SDK's transport is async, which is why this lesson introduces async and await: your tool functions can stay plain def (the SDK runs them on a worker thread), but you need to read async code to follow the SDK.
concept.lowCodeEquivalent: Publishing a flow with an HTTP request trigger and calling it from anywhere with the right headers. The difference is the contract: here the envelope is standardized, so any MCP host already knows how to call you.

pythonBlock.title: Python you need: async and await
pythonBlock.intro: An async function returns a coroutine; await runs it and gives the event loop a chance to serve other requests while this one waits on the network. The SDK's HTTP transport is built from these.
pythonBlock.code:
import anyio
from mcp import Client

async def main() -> None:
    async with Client("http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp") as client:     # connects, negotiates 2026-07-28
        tools = await client.list_tools()                         # await: let others run while we wait
        result = await client.call_tool("find_donor", {"query": "okafor"})
        print([t.name for t in tools.tools], result.structured_content)

anyio.run(main)

# Plain def tools are fine inside MCPServer; the SDK runs them on a worker thread.
# Use async def only when the tool itself awaits something (an async HTTP client).

spec: Implement build_app: build_server(client).streamable_http_app(stateless_http=True, json_response=True). Keep main() serving on 127.0.0.1:$PORT.
Start it and connect with the SDK Client at http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp (the async snippet above). Confirm protocol_version is 2026-07-28.

Send one raw request with httpx: POST /mcp with headers Accept, Content-Type, MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28 and mcp-method: server/discover, body {jsonrpc, id, method: 'server/discover', params: {_meta: {io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities: {}}}}. Read the supportedVersions and serverInfo in the reply.
Send tools/list twice with no session header and confirm both succeed and no MCP-Session-Id header comes back. That is what stateless means on the wire.
askClaudeFor: A walkthrough of what streamable_http_app does with stateless_http=True versus False, and what the mcp-method header is for.
Why the raw request needs the mcp-name header on tools/call (ask it to show you the SDK's modern route code).
writeYourself: build_app, and the raw httpx request script you used to see the envelope (keep it under middleware/scripts/ for yourself).
